messages.subject: Re: Blavaan incredible slow...speed-up solutions?
messages.body_plain:
Sorry for bringing up the speed issue again.

I will teach Bayesian statistics and initially wanted to let participants in the workshop use R. With R, my preference would be blavaan. But speed seems to be an issue?

I have estimated a simple regression model (y ~ x1 + x2, N = approx 2000, item-level missing data less than 5%). Time needed for running this model with Bayesian estimations with diffuse priors is:

blavaan 0.4-3: more than 9 minutes
Stata 17: 10.6 seconds
Mplus 8.8: 1 second

That seems strange: 1 sec with Mplus but nearly 10 minutes with blavaan?  Do these differences make any sense?

CODE:
fit <- bsem("stflife ~ agea + age2", data = data)

Only R and Stata are options for this particular workshop, and I would prefer using R.
(I just tried brms and couldn't even make brms run. But if the source of slow estimation with blavaan lies in Stan, I guess there's no point in trying brms.)

Thanks,
Christopher

The problem is that you get to a missing data pattern with 1 observation, and the sample covariance matrix for that pattern is not positive definite, and then Stan throws an error when you try to model it. I think you can get around it by avoiding the constant terms in the density function.

I've sent data and R code in a separate email. Hopefull, it will be possible to replicate my result.

I want to start teahing with non-informative priors, so no priors were added.

One question, though. I would like to avoid more complex code in RStan, especially when giving an introduction to Bayes. But would using RStan directly be any faster? I understand that the Mplus team has developed some proprietary algorithms that make computations run very fast, also compared to Stata. So I think it's fairer to compare with Stata. Why is RStan/R this much slower than Stata?  (I don't think the implementation of SEM or Bayes is particularly good in Stata, so I would prefer teaching with R and blavaan for this reason too, in addition to the fact that R makes science more accessible than proprietary software does.)

Best,
Chris

messages.subject: Re: Blavaan incredible slow...speed-up solutions?
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for this example. I can reproduce that it is slow (many minutes, when one would hope seconds).

Here is what I think is happening: I have spent time optimizing estimation for bigger models that require SEM software. This has neglected many tricks that can be done for regression (and related models) to speed up model estimation. I know that lavaan flags regression models and does an estimation specific to those models, and this example has made it clear that I need to do the same thing in blavaan.

Stan can be fast for your model. For example, the brms code below uses Stan and finishes in seconds (after model compilation).

library(brms)
mb <- brm(stflife ~ agea + age2, data = data)

With some additions, blavaan should be able to get close to that.

And if you have other slow models that do not qualify as regression, I'd be interested to see those.

Thanks,
Ed

messages.subject: Re: Standardized factor scores
messages.body_plain:
Did you mean how can you scale the factors in the model? Or do you mean how can you save predicted factor scores for each subject? With respect to the former, it's easy to specify in the model fitting process. Here's a 2-factor example:

# 2-factor, 3-indicator model example ----
## specify models ----
null.model <- '
  y1 ~~ y1
  y2 ~~ y2
  y3 ~~ y3
  y4 ~~ y4
  y5 ~~ y5
  y6 ~~ y6
 '
fa.model <- '
  F1 =~ y1 + y2 + y3
  F2 =~ y4 + y5 + y6
  F1 ~~ F2
'
## fit models ----
null.fit <- bcfa(null.model, data=dataframename)
fa.fit <- bcfa(fa.model, data=dataframename, std.lv <http://std.lv>=TRUE) #standardizes the latent variables
fa.fit.postCIs <- blavFitIndices(fa.fit, baseline.model = null.fit)

Best,
Liz

That is a warning message, as opposed to an error, so the function worked but it alerted you that there might be a problem with the results. In this case, if it only gives a warning for p_waic and not for p_loo, then you could use the looic instead of waic. (This all assumes that you are using fitMeasures().)

That warning actually comes from the loo package, which blavaan uses to compute waic and looic. For more detail about what that warning means, see:

Ed

messages.subject_clean: How to convert from blavaan object to a stanfit object?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am using the high performance cluster at my university and the maintainers require us to send each chain as a separate job to the cluster. So if I have four chains, then I will end up with four different fit files.

When I work directly with Stan, I can merge the files using the sflist2stanfit function. However, that doesn't work with blavaan objects.

How can I convert blavaan objects to stanfit objects so that I can use the sflist2stanfit function? Alternatively, how can I merge the resulting files from four different chains?

Note: I ensured that the chains were different by using the bcontrol argument in blavaan and setting the chain ID there, e.g. bcontrol = list(chain_id = 2) for the second chain.

messages.body_plain:
Ibo

Do you understand what are WIAc and LOO? There are bayesian metrics for model comarison. The error messages you are getting are about some minor issue about the calculation of pD, which is a metric of "effectve number of parameters" use by WIAC and LOO, each have a different calculation for their respective pD.

If you use LOO for model comparison, you dont need to pay attention to tjose errors, as they are only related to WIAC. Even woth the low percentage of problems, I wouldnt worry about it.

Further, these are not related to the calculation of factor scores. for that you need to use the blavPredict() function which doesnt use any if these metrics for it

for the blavFitIndices() function, you dont need to worry about this error warning as it uses the LOO metric by default, and your errors are not related to it
